comparison: Perfect agreement on optogenetic identification methodology (C1-C7). Both evaluations find the approach convincing and well-supported. OpenEval provides more technical detail about waveform correlation and validation, while peer reviewers note authors 'adequately responded to all concerns.'

Complete agreement on behavioral performance data (C8-C11). Both accept the task design and performance metrics without concerns. OpenEval notes modest sample sizes, while peer reviewers focus on neural encoding rather than behavioral validation.

Full agreement on DA population dynamics (C12-C15). Both treat these findings as confirmatory of prior literature. Peer reviewers explicitly note this 'confirmed' expected results, while OpenEval emphasizes the extension to GABA neurons.

Strong agreement on trajectory-specific encoding (C16-C19). Both find results convincing. Peer reviewers note this is 'not entirely novel' citing Morris et al. 2006 and Parker et al. 2016, while OpenEval emphasizes the higher GABA engagement (47% vs 21%) as notable.

Partial overlap on GLM regression analysis (C20-C21). OpenEval evaluates the methodological approach to dissecting behavioral variables, while peer reviewers group this with the trajectory encoding findings (C16-C19) as part of the overall convincing results.

Partial agreement on control tasks. OpenEval evaluates the no-delay task (C22-C25) separately, noting modest sample sizes. Peer reviewers combine this with the cue-no-choice task (C26-C29) and highlight memory-dependence as 'an interesting and novel observation' - the paper's key contribution.

Partial agreement on cue-no-choice control task (C26-C29). OpenEval flags the limitation of only 1 GABA animal (C27) as significant for generalizability. Peer reviewers treat this as part of the key novel finding about memory enhancement without noting sample size concerns.

Overlap on main conclusions about memory encoding (C40-C41, C62, C64-C66). OpenEval emphasizes convergence of evidence from multiple approaches. Peer reviewers highlight this as the central novel contribution, stating delay-period activities 'enhanced when task requires short-term memory.'

Strong agreement on reward dissociation (C30-C35, C81). Both accept that trajectory-specific activity reflects memory rather than reward anticipation. OpenEval provides detailed statistical assessment, while peer reviewers accept this as supporting the overall interpretation.

Complete agreement on anatomical localization (C36-C37). Both accept findings without challenge. OpenEval notes the authors' acknowledgment of limitations, while peer reviewers treat this as descriptive observation not affecting main conclusions.

Agreement on sequential activity and multitasking (C68, C70). OpenEval explicitly evaluates these as novel findings evident in heatmaps. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these patterns as part of their overall positive assessment of the study's conclusions.

Agreement on behavioral encoding diversity (C73-C76). OpenEval emphasizes the distinction between population-level constancy and single-neuron selectivity. Peer reviewers accept these conclusions as part of the 'convincing' results about delay-period activity.

Agreement on population-level dynamics (C75). Both note DA populations do not show sustained increases during memory tasks. Peer reviewers explicitly call this 'confirmatory,' while OpenEval integrates it with single-neuron selectivity findings.

Partial overlap on memory-specificity conclusions (C79, C81). OpenEval evaluates cue-no-choice and reward dissociation separately. Peer reviewers group these as supporting the key finding that delay activity is memory-dependent.

Agreement on DA-GABA similarity (C88-C90). Both recognize this as unexpected and important. OpenEval emphasizes the contrast with prior reward/aversion literature, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall convincing results.

Agreement on background literature and knowledge gap (C38-C48). Both accept the framing as appropriate. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of citations, while peer reviewers note consistency with previous studies (Morris et al. 2006, Parker et al. 2016).

Agreement on theoretical frameworks (C49-C53). Both accept the gating theory and persistent activity model citations as appropriate context. OpenEval evaluates accuracy of attributions, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the theoretical framing.

Agreement on network context (C54-C56, C67, C69, C71). Both accept the broader circuit literature as relevant. OpenEval emphasizes the parallel between VTA and cortical encoding, while peer reviewers note the study 'corroborates important findings from recent reports.'

Agreement on VTA GABA background (C57-C61). Both accept the anatomical and methodological context as appropriate. OpenEval notes how the study extends Choi et al. 2020, while peer reviewers do not specifically comment on this literature.

Agreement on motivation and RPE literature (C63, C72, C77-C78, C80). Both accept these citations as providing relevant interpretive framework. OpenEval evaluates accuracy of representations, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the contextual framing.

Agreement on prior DA-GABA differences (C82-C87). Both accept this literature as establishing why current findings are surprising. OpenEval uses this to contextualize the novelty of similar encoding, while peer reviewers do not explicitly comment on these specific citations.

Agreement on co-activity mechanisms (C91-C93). Both accept the anatomical/physiological explanations as plausible. OpenEval notes appropriate caution in C93's speculative framing, while peer reviewers do not specifically address these mechanistic claims.

Agreement on oscillatory mechanisms (C94-C95). Both accept the cited literature on network oscillations. OpenEval notes the inclusion of unpublished observations, while peer reviewers do not specifically comment on these mechanistic proposals.

Agreement on overarching conclusion (C96). Both find the synthesis well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of evidence across multiple analyses, while peer reviewers describe results as 'convincing' and providing 'important results regarding delay-period activity.'
